title: Who protects the UK’s constitutional safeguards?
label: 11 November 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: The committee asked four public servants who oversee standards, civil service conduct and elections how well the UK’s constitutional safeguards work. They described strong foundations, but warned that public trust depends on adequate resources, clear rules and independence. Members challenged whether existing codes and oversight are enough in light of serious public failures. The discussion also covered threats to elections, the need to simplify election law, and the importance of keeping civil servants politically impartial while serving the government of the day.

chapters.title: What these bodies protect
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses see their organisations as safeguards because they help ensure fair public decisions, trusted elections and proper standards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at the organisations that help protect the UK’s constitutional democracy. Do you see your organisations as part of those safeguards?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Yes. The Civil Service Commission oversees civil servants throughout their careers: it checks that appointments are open and based on merit, hears complaints about the Civil Service Code, and advises some people leaving public service about taking jobs in business.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: We also try to prevent problems by explaining what’s expected, not just deal with them after something goes wrong. We don’t, however, decide how much responsibility civil servants should have for their work.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: The Ethics and Integrity Commission doesn’t investigate individual cases or act as a regulator. We advise, educate and look across the standards system, making recommendations based on evidence.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Standards matter because people need confidence that public power is used fairly, without favouritism. Trust also helps sustain people’s acceptance of decisions made by government.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: The Electoral Commission provides independent oversight of elections across the UK. Elections give people a say in who governs and help ensure those in power remain accountable.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Public trust in the conduct of elections is generally high, largely because local authorities run them efficiently. We also work with political parties so they can follow the rules, and we can call out breaches and issue fines.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: People have less confidence in how clearly political money is reported. The bill now before Parliament could improve that. We’re also helping young people understand how elections work, where to find reliable information, and how to disagree with candidates safely.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: Abuse and intimidation are putting people off standing for election. We’re testing teaching materials in about 500 schools and hope to make them available across the UK during 2027.

chapters.title: Pressures on standards and elections
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses identified practical weaknesses—including limited resources, intimidating politics, misleading information and complicated election rules—that could erode trust.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: How well can your organisations carry out these responsibilities, and what gets in the way?

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Our influence depends on producing credible, evidence-based recommendations and on whether government acts on them. Recommendations can take years to become policy. I’m also concerned that new responsibilities may outstrip our staff and funding.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Election safeguards depend on many organisations working together. One serious concern is misleading online content, including foreign attempts to confuse voters or disrupt campaigns. During the May elections, a tool identified 15 cases that we thought threatened democratic integrity.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We can draw attention to this, but we aren’t a specialist technology-monitoring body. We think the state should monitor these threats systematically.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Abuse of candidates is also increasing. Some police forces act well, but others hesitate over where free speech ends and harassment begins. The police have an important role in responding to illegal abuse.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: The public is also concerned that money can buy influence, even though we publish information about where political money comes from. We’re reviewing election spending limits and will give Parliament evidence to help set them.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Election law has become extremely complicated and outdated, with rules layered on top of one another. The new bill adds more detail, though proposals to simplify and combine the rules are also being discussed.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Local authorities are a strength of the system, and I wouldn’t replace them as election organisers. But they’re under pressure and can struggle to find enough staff and resources for this demanding work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the concern isn’t that local authorities shouldn’t run elections, but that they need enough capacity to do it properly?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Exactly. They do a good job, but need the resources to meet the standards required.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Clear, well-written laws can help public bodies work properly. In my time as commissioner, I haven’t experienced undue pressure from politicians or civil servants, though political pressure would probably be harder to manage.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: My term ends in February, but the process to appoint a successor has not yet reached the interview stage. Leaving a vacancy unfilled, or failing to provide a budget, weakens an organisation.

chapters.title: Paper voting, new technology and post-government jobs
chapters.takeaway: The Electoral Commission supports carefully chosen technology but says visible paper ballots protect trust; the rules for former public servants still leave some people outside the system.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Why keep paper voting when technology might make counting easier?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: Paper ballots can be checked openly by candidates, their representatives and election staff. That matters when cyberattacks are common: we receive between 30,000 and 50,000 attacks a month.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: A losing candidate needs to be able to see that the count was fair. That acceptance by those who lose is an important part of trust. Technology can still help with other tasks, such as registering voters or checking people in at polling stations.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: You’ve said the rules on jobs after public service don’t cover some military and intelligence roles. Why is that a concern?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The former advisory committee on business appointments closed a year ago. The Civil Service Commission now handles applications from some senior civil servants and advisers, while the Prime Minister’s independent adviser handles those from politicians.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Some ranks in the Ministry of Defence and intelligence services aren’t covered by our remit. The Cabinet Office owns the rules. We’re reviewing how quickly decisions are made, how risks are assessed and how clearly decisions are published.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Our review found that military officers and staff in some government agencies also fall outside the civil service rules. The Cabinet Office needs to oversee how departments apply the rules, and the rules themselves need updating.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: It’s also important to decide who judges whether a job is in the national interest, so that concerns about former officials benefiting businesses can be properly considered.

chapters.title: Are codes and oversight enough?
chapters.takeaway: Members challenged whether existing standards prevent serious failures; the witnesses agreed that codes only matter when leaders and organisations use them in everyday decisions.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: I hear that the system is in a good place, but serious failures—including infected blood, Hillsborough, the Post Office and Grenfell—make that hard to accept. These happened despite existing codes. Are standards really working, and should central government departments have statutory monitoring officers like local councils?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The Commission oversees recruitment and complaints about the code, but it doesn’t oversee every decision made by departments. Responsibility at the time matters. Civil servants need to be accountable for what they decide, and leaders need to make clear what good performance means.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: A recent staff survey found that 93% of civil servants knew about the code and whom to approach. But awareness alone isn’t enough; leadership and a willingness to act on standards matter.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: I wouldn’t say we’re satisfied. In many inquiries, someone inside the organisation knew something was wrong, but the system became defensive. That damages trust in public institutions, and rebuilding it is important.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: A code shouldn’t just list things people must or mustn’t do. It should shape everyday decisions and remind people of their organisation’s purpose. Different organisations may need different codes, developed with staff and the people affected by their work.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: The proposed Public Office (Accountability) Bill would require public bodies to have codes of ethical conduct. We can help them write and put those codes into practice, but a standard template won’t work for everyone.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: I haven’t examined the case for monitoring officers in central government, but I’ll take that away and look at it.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: I’m also concerned that civil servants can formally challenge a minister’s decision on value for money, but not necessarily on standards. If standards matter, shouldn’t that question be examined too?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: I’d need to think about the wider implications before answering that.

chapters.title: Independence and an impartial civil service
chapters.takeaway: Legal backing can protect independence and enforcement, but it can also make rules slow to change; civil servants must give professional advice while ultimately serving the elected government.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: Does it help for these bodies to be established by law? And does strong leadership risk making the Civil Service less politically impartial?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: The Electoral Commission needs legal authority because it regulates elections and can issue penalties. But changing laws takes time, while threats and technology change quickly. The answer is to write laws that can keep working as circumstances change, and to update them when needed.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Bodies that investigate cases or impose penalties need legal protection to act fairly and independently. But having a law isn’t enough: the law covering lobbyists, for example, is so limited that only a small share of lobbying is registered.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Our own independence depends on being able to choose our work and publish our conclusions freely. We’re accountable to Parliament, but we still rely on the Cabinet Office for staff, accommodation and funding.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: The adviser on ministerial interests now has a substantial role, including investigations and advice on jobs after ministers leave office. I think that role should be established by law.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The Commission’s legal basis helps protect fair recruitment. For example, the law says special advisers can’t take part in appointing civil servants, so we can require them to leave a selection process.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Impartiality doesn’t mean civil servants have no personal views. It means that, at work, they act as professionals and serve the government elected at the time. If someone can’t do that, they may decide that the profession isn’t right for them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Civil servants must explain what can be done and warn ministers about risks. The government of the day ultimately decides, but the Civil Service provides continuity when governments change.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Should the Civil Service also protect its ability to serve future governments, if a minister asks for something that could damage that ability?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: One way to make a serious concern clear is for a senior civil servant to ask for a formal ministerial direction. That records that the official believes the action is wrong but will follow the instruction if required.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: Is the impartiality of the Civil Service under threat?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: It’s always contested, and it should be discussed. Democracy requires both the elected government’s authority and a Civil Service that can offer caution and continuity. The system can work if these bodies have the resources and freedom to do their jobs.

chapters.title: Election law and future choices
chapters.takeaway: The Electoral Commission expects the election bill to require major preparation, wants stronger powers to investigate suspicious activity, and says compulsory voting needs fresh evidence before Britain can judge it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What’s missing from the Representation of the People Bill, and how are you preparing for it?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: It will be a major part of our work in 2027 and 2028. We’ll take on new responsibilities for regulating candidates and need systems to help tens of thousands of candidates understand the rules.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: The bill also introduces changes to voting at 16 and voter registration. It will require many detailed rules to be made afterwards, because election law is spread across so many measures. We’d like the Law Commission to bring the rules together and make them easier to use.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: We’d also like broader powers to obtain information when we’re checking whether someone outside the regulated system has broken the rules, or when a concern involves money not covered by party accounts. The new rules will be hard to enforce without that information.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Should the Electoral Commission be able to prosecute people itself?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: We’re not seeking the power to bring private prosecutions. We use data to identify suspicious patterns and give evidence to the police or other authorities, which have the specialist powers needed to investigate and prosecute crimes.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: Have you considered compulsory voting, as used in Australia?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We last looked at it about 15 years ago. We’d want to gather current evidence and consider whether it would work in Britain before taking a view.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: Australia’s compulsory voting sits on top of a much broader system: it works hard to register everyone and spends heavily to encourage people to vote. Britain is behind on registration, though the bill could help us improve. Once we’ve strengthened those basics, we’ll be in a better position to judge whether compulsory voting makes sense here.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We’d also need to consider what compulsory voting would mean in the British context and whether the public would support the cost and the requirement. We need evidence before advising.
